lead: A DNA biosensor answers one narrow question: does this sample contain a strand with a known sequence? It holds the complementary strand, the probe, on an electrode and lets the target hybridise to it. The duplex formed is then read as a current or an impedance change. The same trick serves pathogen detection, mutation screening, forensic samples and food authenticity checks, and it is the reason a single wrong base can be caught.
prereq: You need: 4.2 for nucleic acid probes and hybridisation, and 4.3 for electrode transduction.

blocks.text: The sensor carries the complementary strand, the probe, fixed on the transducer. The probe is a single synthetic strand of 15–30 bases. Shorter than 15 and the duplex is too weak, so near-matches bind too; longer than 30 and one wrong base changes the stability too little to see.

Anchoring uses a thiol group (–SH) at the probe's 5' end. Clean gold dipped in probe solution forms Au–S bonds, and the strands pack into a self-assembled monolayer (SAM): one molecule thick, held by the sulphur head, bases free in the buffer.

items: Polish the gold electrode, rinse with water and dry.
Immerse in 0.1–1 µM thiolated probe in buffer for 1–16 hours.
Rinse, then backfill with 1 mM 6-mercapto-1-hexanol for about one hour.
Rinse, store wet at 4 °C and use within days.

blocks.text: The backfill thiol, MCH, fills bare gold between probes. It stands the probes upright instead of letting them lie flat, spaces them so a target can reach in, and blocks the metal so redox molecules in solution cannot touch it and add background current. Many probes also carry a block of ten thymine bases (T10) between the thiol anchor and the sequence, a linker that holds the probe away from the gold; the MCH backfill is still done.

Sample DNA arrives double-stranded. Heat it to 95 °C for five minutes and cool it fast on ice; the strands separate and stay apart, and these single strands are added to the electrode. Bases then pair by Watson–Crick rules: A with T through two hydrogen bonds, G with C through three. A G+C-rich duplex is therefore more stable than an A+T-rich one of the same length.

blocks.where: A, T, G, C are the counts of each base in the probe (not percentages); Tm is the melting temperature in °C, at which half the duplex has separated.

blocks.text: Salt matters. Na⁺ ions shield the negative phosphate backbones, which otherwise repel each other, so low salt destabilises the duplex. Formamide, a denaturant, lowers Tm and lets an assay run cooler. The Wallace rule above is a counting rule for perfect-match probes of about 14–20 bases in high-salt buffer; for longer probes, locked nucleic acids or mixed solvents, use a nearest-neighbour calculation.

The wash gives selectivity. After hybridisation, wash the electrode at Tm − 5 °C in the same buffer. A perfectly matched target stays bound; a target with one internal mismatch has a Tm about 5 °C lower, so at the wash temperature about half of it has separated and the wash carries those strands away. This strictness is stringency, set by temperature and salt together. Wash too cold or too salty and mismatches survive, giving a false positive.

sections.h3: Reading the duplex: label-free and labelled

blocks.text: A duplex changes the electrode surface, and several transducers can report it.

items: Impedance: the negative backbone of the duplex repels ferri/ferrocyanide ions, so charge-transfer resistance rises as duplex forms.
ISFET: the extra surface charge shifts the threshold voltage (see 4.4).
Surface plasmon resonance: the added mass changes the refractive index at a gold film, read as an angle shift.

blocks.text: Labelled routes give a bigger signal for extra steps. A redox-active intercalator such as methylene blue is added after hybridisation; it binds only duplex DNA, so more duplex means more bound dye and a larger current after rinsing. A ferrocene tag on the target, or on a signalling probe, is present all the time, but it is held at the electrode and gives current only when the target is captured in a duplex; unbound tagged strands are washed away. An enzyme label such as horseradish peroxidase turns one binding event into many electrons through substrate turnover. The sandwich format uses a capture probe on the electrode plus a labelled detector probe binding a second site on the target, which adds specificity but needs a longer target.

The stem-loop (E-DNA) probe is a neat alternative. Its two ends are self-complementary and pair with each other, holding a redox tag close to the electrode so current flows freely. Target binding opens the stem, the tag swings away and the current falls. That is a signal-off sensor: probe loss or damage lowers the current exactly as target does, so always normalise.

In clean buffer a label-free electrode reaches picomolar. A real sample — blood, sputum, a food rinse — holds femtomolar target among far more non-target DNA, so most assays amplify first with PCR or an isothermal method such as LAMP or RPA.

Pathogen detection covers tuberculosis, dengue and Salmonella in food and water. Mutation screening covers known single-base changes, where the stringency wash is the entire method. Forensic work uses short mitochondrial or repeat-region sequences from tiny degraded samples. Food authenticity checks identify species in meat and fish.

Every assay runs three electrodes: a blank, a perfect-match positive and a single-mismatch negative. A strong current alone proves nothing; it must exceed the mismatch signal by a margin you have calibrated (4.1).

spec.aria: Gold strip with five probe strands standing on thiol heads, short backfill molecules between them, one probe paired with a target strand, and beside it three bars of charge-transfer resistance, 1.26, 1.56 and 3.00 kilo-ohms, over a dashed baseline at 1.20.

examples.question: The probe 5'-ATGCTAGCTAGGCATCGATC-3' is immobilised on a gold electrode. (a) Count each base and find the melting temperature with the Wallace rule. (b) State a suitable hybridisation temperature. (c) Estimate the melting temperature of a target carrying one internal mismatch and say what a wash at the hybridisation temperature does to each duplex.
steps: Count the bases in the 20-base sequence: A = 5, T = 5, G = 5, C = 5. Check: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 bases.
Hybridise 5 °C below Tm: 60 − 5 = 55 °C, in buffer with enough salt to keep the duplex stable.
One internal mismatch lowers Tm by about 5 °C, so the mismatched duplex has Tm ≈ 60 − 5 = 55 °C.

At the 55 °C wash the matched duplex (Tm 60 °C) is mostly still paired. The mismatched duplex is at its own Tm, so about half of it has separated, and the wash removes those strands; the matched signal is therefore clearly larger than the mismatch signal. Washing a little hotter, or in lower salt, widens the gap.
The 50 % G+C content is what sets Tm at 60 °C; the hybridisation and wash temperatures then follow from Tm, not from the G+C content directly.
examples.answer: Tm = 60 °C, so hybridise and wash at 55 °C for this probe; a one-base mismatch has Tm ≈ 55 °C, about half of it is washed off, and the perfect match stays mostly bound.

examples.question: A probe electrode in ferri/ferrocyanide has a charge-transfer resistance R<sub>ct</sub> of 1.20 kΩ. After hybridisation and washing, R<sub>ct</sub> is 1.26 kΩ for a blank, 1.56 kΩ for a one-mismatch target and 3.00 kΩ for the matched target. Find the relative change for each and the matched-to-mismatch ratio.
steps: Relative change = (R<sub>ct</sub> − R<sub>ct,0</sub>) ÷ R<sub>ct,0</sub>, with R<sub>ct,0</sub> = 1.20 kΩ.
examples.answer: Blank 5 %, mismatch 30 %, match 150 %; the matched signal is five times the mismatch signal, so a decision threshold between them (for example 75 %) separates the two.

traps: Using the Wallace rule on a 60-base probe or on locked-nucleic-acid probes; it is a count for 14–20 base perfect matches in high-salt buffer only.
Reporting a hybridisation signal as proof of the target without a mismatched control probe on the same chip; non-specific adsorption also gives current.
Copying a wash temperature from a paper without copying the salt: the same probe has a different Tm in 0.1 M and 1 M Na⁺.
Swapping probe and target in the answer: the probe is fixed and known, the target is what the sample brings.
Forgetting that E-DNA is signal-off, so probe loss looks like a positive unless the current is normalised to a redox standard.

quiz.q: Define Tm of a DNA duplex.
quiz.a: The temperature in °C at which half of the duplex molecules have separated into single strands.

quiz.q: Why is the gold backfilled with MCH after probe immobilisation?
quiz.a: It stands the probes upright, spaces them so target can reach in, and blocks bare gold so solution redox species do not add background current.

quiz.q: A probe is 18 bases long with A = 4, T = 5, G = 4, C = 5. Find Tm and a hybridisation temperature.
A 20-base probe with Tm 60 °C gives a large current with the matched target and a smaller but still clear current with a one-mismatch target after a 50 °C wash. What do you change?
quiz.a: Raise the wash temperature towards 55 °C, and if needed lower the salt, so most of the mismatched target is removed while the matched duplex stays.

quiz.q: An E-DNA sensor's current drops after sample addition. Give one target-related and one artefact explanation, and the control that separates them.
quiz.a: Target binding opens the stem and moves the tag away; alternatively probe is lost or degraded. A mismatch control probe plus normalisation to a redox standard separates the two.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cartridge systems that lyse, amplify and detect on one chip now run DNA tests at the point of care, and CRISPR-linked reporters and nanopore sequencing are the newer routes. Search for 'E-DNA sensor' and 'isothermal amplification LAMP' to go further.
